scenes.narration: Could you find this shape's area without measuring any side? Its corners sit on a square grid with unit spacing. Count the dots strictly inside: six. Now count the dots on the boundary: twelve. Include points along an edge, not just the corners. Those two counts are enough. Six, plus half of twelve, minus one. The area is eleven square units. This is Pick's theorem. Let us see why the recipe is more than a lucky guess.

Try a rectangle first: four units across and three units high. Its area is twelve. Inside, there are three columns of two dots: six interior points. On the boundary, there are fourteen distinct dots. Corners count once. Six plus seven minus one gives twelve. For a rectangle of any whole-number width and height, the same counting works. Interior points contribute the missing inner rectangle; half the boundary restores the edge strips; subtracting one fixes the corner count.

Here is the useful structural idea. Split a square along a diagonal. When the two triangles meet, their shared edge disappears from the outside boundary. The endpoints stay on the outer boundary, but points strictly between them become interior points. Pick's counting rule compensates for exactly that change, so its values add just like areas. This is a glimpse of the proof, not the whole proof. Completing it extends the formula from rectangles to triangles, then to ordinary lattice polygons.

Now move this corner one grid step outward. The shape changes, but you can still count. There are eight interior points and twelve boundary points. Eight plus six minus one gives thirteen square units. Two extra units appeared without measuring a sloping edge. The conditions matter: a simple polygon, grid-point vertices, and no holes. Curved edges or a corner between grid points break this recipe. Sometimes the easiest way to measure a region is to count what sits inside and around it.
